uni-biotech-core.title: Biotechnology core
uni-biotech-core.description: Core B.Tech/B.Sc biotechnology: molecular biology, genetic engineering, bioprocess engineering, bioinformatics with small Python labs, and enzyme kinetics, with solved numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian degree programmes.

courses.title: Molecular biology: central dogma with code labs
courses.summary: DNA structure, transcription and translation worked through base-pair arithmetic and short Python programs.

lessons.title: Lab: Base composition with Chargaff's rules

scenes.text: A forensic trainee in Hyderabad is told a double-stranded DNA sample has 30% adenine.
She must predict guanine content.

steps.title: Chargaff
steps.body: In double-stranded DNA, **A = T** and **G = C**, so A + G = 50% of bases.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Rules do not hold for single-stranded DNA or RNA.

activity.prompt: A double-stranded DNA sample has 30% adenine. What is the % guanine?

scenes.text: RNA polymerase copies the coding strand into mRNA, using U in place of T.
You automate it in Python.

steps.title: Coding strand
steps.body: The mRNA has the same sequence as the coding (non-template) strand with T replaced by U.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ATGGCCAAA → AUGGCCAAA.

steps.title: Template
steps.body: The template strand is its complement and reads 3'→5'.

activity.prompt: Print the mRNA for the coding strand stored in seq (replace T with U).

scenes.text: Each three-base codon codes for one amino acid.
A stop codon ends translation.

steps.title: Genetic code
steps.body: AUG codes for Met (start). UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. The code is degenerate (many codons per amino acid) but unambiguous.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: AUG GCU GAA UAA → Met–Ala–Glu–stop, written MAE.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: A single-base insertion shifts the reading frame; the downstream protein usually becomes nonsense.

steps.body: Genome annotation scans all six frames, including the reverse strand.

story.title: Cloning a gene into a plasmid

scenes.text: A start-up team clones a reporter gene into an E. coli vector.
The protocol steps have been shuffled.

steps.title: Typical workflow
steps.body: Amplify insert, cut insert and vector, ligate, transform, select, verify.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: Antibiotic resistance on the vector lets only transformed cells grow on selective plates.

steps.title: Biosafety
steps.body: Work follows institutional biosafety rules and approved organisms only.

scenes.text: After transformation the plate has blue and white colonies on X-gal/IPTG/ampicillin.
You choose which colonies to pick.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: Insertion into lacZα disrupts β-galactosidase: recombinant colonies are white; empty vectors give blue.

steps.title: Reading
steps.body: No growth = not transformed; blue = vector without insert; white = likely recombinant.

steps.title: Verify
steps.body: Satellite colonies and false whites occur, so confirm by PCR.

a.text: The plate shows many blue colonies and a few white ones. What do you pick?

choices.feedback: Correct: white colonies likely carry an insert.

choices.label: Pick blue colonies
choices.feedback: Blue colonies have intact lacZα (no insert).

good.text: Colony PCR confirms the insert in 5 of 6 clones. Experiment proceeds to sequencing.

bad.text: Sequencing shows empty vector only. A day is lost.

courses.title: Bioinformatics with Python: sequences, alignment scores and k-mers
courses.summary: GC content, reverse complement, Hamming distance and k-mer counting in short deterministic Python programs.

scenes.text: Higher GC content gives more stable DNA.
You write a one-liner to report it for primer design.

steps.title: Why GC matters
steps.body: G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, so GC-rich DNA melts at a higher temperature.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ATGCGCGA has 5 G/C of 8 bases = 62.5%.

steps.title: Python
steps.body: Count with sum(1 for b in s if b in 'GC').

activity.prompt: Print the GC content of seq as a percentage with one decimal place.
activity.solution:
seq = "ATGCGCGA"
gc = sum(1 for b in seq if b in "GC")
print(f"{100*gc/len(seq):.1f}")

scenes.text: A reverse primer anneals to the other strand.
You compute the reverse complement of a target.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Complement each base (A↔T, G↔C) and reverse the order so the new strand reads 5'→3'.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ATGCGC → complement TACGCG → reverse GCGCAT.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Complement without reversing gives the wrong 5'→3' direction.

activity.prompt: Print the reverse complement of seq.

story.title: How different are these two reads?

scenes.text: Two equal-length reads from different samples need comparison.
Count mismatching positions.

steps.title: Hamming distance
steps.body: Number of positions where equal-length strings differ. It ignores insertions and deletions.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: GATTACA vs GACTATA differ at positions 3 and 6 → 2.

steps.title: Beyond
steps.body: Edit distance allows gaps and underlies sequence alignment.

activity.prompt: Print the Hamming distance between a and b.
activity.solution:
a = "GATTACA"
b = "GACTATA"
print(sum(1 for x, y in zip(a, b) if x != y))

scenes.text: Tandem repeats appear as over-represented k-mers.
You build a k-mer counter.

steps.title: k-mers
steps.body: A k-mer is a substring of length k. Sliding window of step 1 gives len − k + 1 k-mers.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ATATATGC has 7 2-mers: AT, TA, AT, TA, AT, TG, GC → AT = 3.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: k-mer counts power genome assemblers and alignment-free comparison.

activity.prompt: Count all 2-mers in seq and print the most frequent one and its count as 'KMER COUNT'.
activity.starter:
seq = "ATATATGC"
counts = {}
# fill counts
best = max(counts, key=counts.get)
print(best, counts[best])
activity.solution:
seq = "ATATATGC"
counts = {}
for i in range(len(seq) - 1):
    k = seq[i:i+2]
    counts[k] = counts.get(k, 0) + 1
best = max(counts, key=counts.get)
print(best, counts[best])

courses.title: Enzyme kinetics: Michaelis–Menten and inhibition
courses.summary: Michaelis–Menten rates, competitive inhibition and catalytic efficiency.
outcomes: Compute v from Vmax and Km

scenes.text: An enzyme has Vmax 100 µmol/min and Km 2 mM.
A student predicts rate at 2 mM substrate.

steps.title: Equation
steps.body: **v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S])**; at [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Km is a concentration, not a rate.

activity.prompt: Vmax = 100 µmol/min, Km = 2 mM, [S] = 2 mM. Rate v?

quiz.q: At very high [S] the rate approaches

scenes.text: The same enzyme is assayed at 18 mM.
You check the saturation.

steps.title: Fraction
steps.body: 90% of Vmax at [S] = 9 Km.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: It takes about 9 Km to reach 90% Vmax.

activity.prompt: Vmax = 100 µmol/min, Km = 2 mM, [S] = 18 mM. Rate?

story.title: A drug blocks the active site

scenes.text: An inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site, with Ki = 2 mM at 4 mM concentration.
You predict apparent Km.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Competitive: **Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki)**; Vmax unchanged.

steps.title: Overcoming
steps.body: High substrate can outcompete a competitive inhibitor.

activity.prompt: Km = 2 mM, [I] = 4 mM, Ki = 2 mM. Apparent Km?

scenes.text: A start-up compares two engineered variants.
They want kcat and efficiency.

steps.title: kcat
steps.body: **kcat = Vmax/[E]total**; catalytic efficiency is kcat/Km.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Vmax = 120 µM/s, [E] = 0.4 µM → kcat = 300 s⁻¹. With Km = 150 µM, kcat/Km = 2 µM⁻¹s⁻¹ = 2×10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹.

steps.title: Limit
steps.body: Diffusion limits kcat/Km to about 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹.
